scenarios.title: Scenario 5 — Claude Code for Continuous Integration
scenarios.brief: A travel-booking company runs Claude Code in GitHub Actions on a Kotlin and TypeScript repository. It has four jobs: a pull-request review that posts inline comments, an autofix job for failing builds, test generation for new endpoints, and a weekly dependency-risk report. The review job uses an MCP server for code search and API guidelines. CLAUDE.md and .claude/ are committed.

questions.question: The review job runs claude "Check this diff for injection risks" in a workflow step. The engineer tested it in a terminal, where she read the answer and typed /exit. On the runner, the step sits idle until the job's time limit cancels it. The next step, which turns the reply into comments, then has nothing to read. What should the review step run instead?

options.t: Wrap the command in an expect script that sends /exit once the answer appears.
options.why: Works, but a workaround. It fakes the person at the keyboard, and it must guess when the answer is finished. The CLI already has a mode that needs no person.

options.t: Set a short time limit on the step so a stuck run fails within minutes, not hours.
options.why: Works, but hides the problem. The job fails sooner and wastes fewer runner hours, but it still produces no review.

options.t: Run claude -p with the same prompt, and have the next step read its standard output.
options.why: Best. -p (--print) is non-interactive mode: Claude answers once, prints the reply and exits, so nothing waits for a person.

options.t: Replace the step with a script that sends the diff to the Messages API and prints the reply.
options.why: Works, but overbuilt. A direct API call does finish, but it rebuilds the job by hand and gives up the Claude Code setup the repository already commits.

questions.decider: The engineer tested it in a terminal, where she read the answer and typed /exit.
questions.explanation: In CI, Claude Code runs in print mode (-p / --print): one prompt in, one answer out, then exit. Without it the CLI waits for a person to type the next turn.

eli5.question: A command that worked in a terminal hangs forever in CI. The clue: in the terminal, a person typed /exit to finish it. On the runner, nobody is there to type.
eli5.answer: Think of a phone call that only ends when someone hangs up. In a terminal, the engineer hung up by typing /exit. In CI nobody is on the line, so the call stays open. Claude Code has a “leave a message” mode instead: claude -p (print mode) answers once, prints the reply and hangs up by itself. Rule: Claude Code in a script or CI → always use -p.
options: A robot that hangs up for you works, but it has to guess when the other side is done talking.
Cutting the call off sooner saves time, but you still get no message.
Correct. Leave-a-message mode: answer once, then hang up by itself.
Writing your own phone works, but you already own one with the right button.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think a hang in CI needs a timeout or a trick to end the session. The real cause is simpler: plain claude "..." starts an interactive session that waits for the next turn. The supported answer is print mode, -p, which is built for scripts.
deep.diagram:
claude "..."     → answers, then waits for input (hang)
claude -p "..."  → answers, prints, exits (CI-safe)

deep.rule: Claude Code in a pipeline → claude -p. It answers once and exits.

questions.trap: More context or reasoning instead of structure
questions.question: The review job runs claude -p, and its findings come back as markdown. A Python script uses regular expressions to pull out the file, line and message for each inline comment. Some comments land on the wrong line. On some runs nothing posts, because a heading came back in a style the patterns don't expect. Only the script reads this output. What is the best fix?

options.t: Add two sample findings to the prompt, in the exact heading and bullet style the patterns expect.
options.why: Works, but only usually. Examples make the layout steadier, but the script still parses prose, and the next unexpected shape breaks it again.

options.t: Add --output-format json and a --json-schema with file, line, severity and message.
options.why: Best. A program is the only reader, so it should get named fields, not prose to re-parse. The schema makes file and line values instead of patterns to guess.

options.t: Make the patterns accept more heading and list styles, with a test for each failure seen so far.
options.why: Works, but treats the symptom. Each fix covers one shape the script has already met, and the next new shape fails again.

options.t: Review each changed file in its own run, so the script knows the file and parses only line and message.
options.why: Works, but different problem. Per-file runs help attention on big diffs, but line and message are still pulled out of free text.

questions.decider: Only the script reads this output.
questions.explanation: When a program consumes Claude Code output in CI, declare its shape: --output-format json with --json-schema gives the posting script fields to read instead of prose to parse.

eli5.question: A script reads Claude's markdown with patterns and keeps breaking. The clue: only the script reads this output, so nobody needs nice prose.
eli5.answer: Asking someone to write a letter you then cut up with scissors is fragile. Handing them a form with labelled boxes is not. For Claude Code the form is --output-format json plus a --json-schema naming the boxes: file, line, severity, message. Rule: a program reads it → structured output from the CLI, not prose.
options: A sample letter helps the writer, but you are still cutting up letters.
Correct. A form with labelled boxes the script can read directly.
Sharper scissors cut the letters you've seen; the next odd letter still tears.
One letter per file is shorter, but it is still a letter to cut up.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think parsing failures mean the prose needs to be more regular, through examples or better patterns. That is still parsing prose. When a program is the only reader, the CLI can hand it structured output: JSON whose fields a schema fixes.

questions.question: The test generator keeps writing tests for generated API client code, which the team leaves untested on purpose. It also uses mock factories that the team replaced with builders last year. Developers get the same advice from Claude Code on their laptops. The testing conventions are already written up in docs/testing.md, which the platform team keeps current. Where should the fix go?

options.t: In the test generator's workflow step, as testing conventions passed with --append-system-prompt.
options.why: Works, but covers only CI. The generator would improve, but laptops keep the old advice, and a second copy lives in a workflow file.

options.t: In a project skill in .claude/skills/testing/ that the generator's prompt invokes.
options.why: Works, but only when invoked. CI would call it, but developers on laptops must remember to, and standards should apply in every session.

options.t: In a .claude/rules/ file with a copy of the conventions and paths: for test files.
options.why: Works, but a second copy. It would load for test files everywhere, but it duplicates a document the platform team already maintains, and the two drift.

options.t: In the committed project CLAUDE.md, as an @import of docs/testing.md.
options.why: Best. Project memory loads in every Claude Code session in the repository, in CI and on laptops. The import reuses the document the platform team already keeps current.

questions.decider: The testing conventions are already written up in docs/testing.md, which the platform team keeps current.
questions.explanation: CLAUDE.md is where a repository gives every Claude Code session its testing standards and fixtures, in CI and locally. @import lets it reference an existing document instead of copying it.

eli5.question: Claude writes outdated tests both in CI and on laptops. The team already has a good testing guide. The clue: everyone gets the bad advice, and the guide already exists.
eli5.answer: The team already has a handbook, but nobody gave Claude a copy. The fix is to clip the handbook into the team's noticeboard, the committed project CLAUDE.md, with an @import line. Every session reads the noticeboard, and the platform team keeps editing the one handbook. Rule: project standards → project CLAUDE.md, and @import a document that already exists.
options: Telling only the CI worker fixes CI; people on laptops still get the old advice.
A manual someone has to open helps only the people who remember to open it.
A photocopy pinned by the test files works until the handbook changes and the copy doesn't.
Correct. Pin the real handbook to the board everyone reads.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think a CI problem needs a CI fix. Laptops show the same wrong advice, so the gap is in the project context every session shares. That is the job of the committed project CLAUDE.md, and @import lets it point at the document the team already maintains.
deep.diagram:
CLAUDE.md:  @docs/testing.md
  → CI test job, CI review, every laptop session

questions.question: To save a runner start-up, one claude -p call does two jobs. It writes tests for the new endpoints, then reviews the whole pull request, new tests included. Human reviewers keep finding generated tests that assert on the wrong thing. The automated review has not flagged one of them. Its prompt lists only general quality checks. What would most improve the review of generated tests?

options.t: Run the review as a separate claude -p call that gets the diff but no generation turns.
options.why: Best. The combined session still holds the reasoning that wrote the tests, so it reads them as settled. A fresh instance checks them the way the human reviewers do.

options.t: Add a review check that each assertion tests the behaviour that the test's name describes.
options.why: Works, but leaves the cause. Explicit criteria help any reviewer, but this reviewer is checking tests it has just decided were right.

options.t: Turn on extended thinking for the review half, with room to re-derive each test's intent.
options.why: Works, but same blind spot. More reasoning in the same context still starts from the generation reasoning.

options.t: Split the review into per-file passes plus one cross-file pass over source and new tests.
options.why: Works, but different problem. Multi-pass review fixes thin attention on large diffs. The problem here is that the reviewer wrote what it reviews.

questions.decider: one claude -p call does two jobs
questions.explanation: A session is a weak reviewer of its own output, because it keeps the reasoning that produced it. An independent instance with no generation history catches more than self-review, even with extended thinking.

eli5.question: The same Claude call writes tests and then reviews them, and its review never finds the bad tests humans find. The clue: one call does two jobs.
eli5.answer: Marking your own homework rarely finds your mistakes: you read what you meant, not what you wrote. A different marker catches them. Here that means a separate claude -p call that sees the diff but not the reasoning that wrote the tests (an independent review instance). Rule: never let the writer review its own work in the same session.
options: Correct. A fresh marker who never saw the working.
A sharper marking scheme helps, but the student is still marking their own homework.
Thinking longer about your own answers mostly convinces you they're right.
Marking page by page helps with long homework, but it's still your own homework.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think a review that misses problems needs better criteria or more thinking. Those help an independent reviewer. Here the reviewer is the same session that wrote the tests, so it keeps the reasoning behind them and tends to agree with itself. The fix is who reviews.
deep.diagram:
now:  one session: write tests → review PR → approve
fix:  session A writes → fresh claude -p reviews diff

questions.question: Developers act on few of the review's findings. The biggest group says a doc comment is out of date, and most of those comments are fine. That group comes from one prompt line: “keep code documentation trustworthy”. Developers now skim past the whole review, including its accurate security findings. What change most improves precision?

options.t: Add three sample findings of stale doc comments, each with its file, line and suggested fix.
options.why: Works, but too early. Examples steady the shape of findings, but they rest on a goal with no boundary, so Claude still guesses what counts.

options.t: Have a second instance score each finding, and post only the ones it rates high.
options.why: Works, but overbuilt. A grader cuts some noise, but it judges against the same vague “trustworthy” and doubles the cost of every review.

options.t: Reword that line: flag a doc comment only when what it claims differs from what the code does.
options.why: Best. “Trustworthy” has no boundary, so almost any comment can be flagged. A condition comparing claim and code can be checked, and explicit criteria are what raise precision.

options.t: Post doc-comment findings in a folded summary at the end, not as inline comments.
options.why: Works, but hides the problem. Security findings stand out again, but the doc-comment findings are as wrong as before.

questions.decider: That group comes from one prompt line: “keep code documentation trustworthy”.
questions.explanation: Vague goals produce vague findings. Replace a goal like “trustworthy” with a condition checkable against the code, because a noisy category erodes trust in the accurate findings too.

eli5.question: One vague prompt line creates lots of wrong findings, and people now ignore the whole review. The clue: the line says trustworthy, which has no clear edge.
eli5.answer: Telling a proofreader “make sure the captions are good” gets every caption flagged. Telling them “flag a caption only when it describes something not in the picture” gets the real errors. That is an explicit criterion: a test Claude can check against the code. Rule: replace vague goals with conditions you can check.
options: Showing sample corrections helps, but the proofreader still doesn't know which captions count.
A second proofreader with the same vague brief is just as unsure, and twice the cost.
Correct. Give a test: flag it only when the words don't match the picture.
Moving the corrections to the back hides them, but they are still wrong.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think a noisy category needs examples, a filter or a quieter place. Those treat its output. The cause is the instruction: “trustworthy” has no boundary. The exam guide's fix is an explicit criterion, for example flag a comment only when its claim contradicts the code.

questions.trap: More context or reasoning instead of structure
questions.question: The review prompt defines each severity level with a clear test, such as “reachable from an unauthenticated request”. Most findings get the same level on every run. A possible null dereference on a guarded path was marked critical on one pull request and minor on another. The swings happen where two of the tests seem to apply at once. What most improves consistency?

options.t: Add more conditions to each level's definition to cover guarded and partly guarded paths.
options.why: Works, but more of the same. Sharper wording helps when levels are vague. These are already clear tests, and more conditions add more to weigh at the boundary.

options.t: Add a few borderline findings, each with the level chosen and why the other level lost.
options.why: Best. The written tests are fine; the inconsistency sits where two of them overlap. Examples that show the reasoning on borderline cases make those calls consistent.

options.t: Run the review three times, and post each finding at the level most runs gave it.
options.why: Works, but overbuilt. Voting smooths some swings, but it triples the cost of a check developers wait on, and it hides the boundary rather than teaching it.

options.t: Ask Claude to reason step by step through each test before it picks a level.
options.why: Works, but only usually. Reasoning helps a little, but at the boundary two tests still fit, and Claude has nothing showing which one wins.

questions.decider: The swings happen where two of the tests seem to apply at once.
questions.explanation: When instructions are already explicit but output still varies on borderline cases, few-shot examples are the most effective fix. Choose boundary cases and show why one level beat the other.

eli5.question: Severity rules are clear and work most of the time, but borderline findings flip between levels. The clue: the swings happen where two tests apply at once.
eli5.answer: A referee who knows the rulebook still calls borderline fouls differently. What helps is watching replays of borderline calls with the reason for each decision. For Claude, those replays are few-shot examples: a few boundary findings, each with the level chosen and why the other lost. Rule: clear rules but inconsistent borderline calls → show worked examples.
options: A thicker rulebook gives the referee more rules to weigh against each other.
Correct. Replays of borderline calls, with the reason for each.
Three referees voting smooths some calls, at three times the cost, and none of them learns the boundary.
Thinking harder helps a little, but two rules still fit and nothing shows which wins.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think inconsistent output means the rules need more words. Here the rules are clear tests and work on most findings. The swings sit at the overlap between two tests. The exam guide's fix for that is few-shot examples that show the reasoning on ambiguous cases.

questions.question: Finance wants the Message Batches discount used wherever it fits. Three jobs cost the most. The pull-request review is a required check, and developers wait for it before they can merge. A new nightly flaky-test summary is read at the morning stand-up. The weekly dependency-risk report is read at Monday planning. Which plan should the team adopt?

options.t: Batch the nightly summary and the weekly report, and keep the review on real-time calls.
options.why: Best. The summary and the report are read hours later, so they take the discount. The review blocks a merge while someone waits, and batches promise no response time.

options.t: Batch all three, and have the review job poll for its result before it posts a status.
options.why: Works, but blocks the merge. It saves the most, but batches can take up to a day with no latency promise, and the merge button waits that long.

options.t: Batch only the weekly report, and keep the nightly summary and review on real-time calls.
options.why: Works, but misses savings. The report is a good fit, but the overnight summary is too, and it stays at full price.

options.t: Batch all three, and fall back to a real-time call when a review result is slow.
options.why: Works, but overbuilt. For the blocking review the fallback would fire on most runs, so the team pays for both paths and keeps two code paths.

questions.decider: The pull-request review is a required check, and developers wait for it before they can merge.
questions.explanation: Message Batches save 50% but can take up to 24 hours with no latency guarantee. They suit overnight and weekly work, not checks that block a merge.

eli5.question: Finance wants the cheap, slow option wherever it fits. The clue: developers wait for the review before they can merge; nobody waits for the summary or the report.
eli5.answer: Overnight post is half price but arrives whenever it arrives. It's fine for a letter read next week, not for a key someone is standing at the door waiting for. The Message Batches API is that overnight post: half price, up to a day, no promised time. Rule: someone waiting → real-time. Read later → batch.
options: Correct. Send the two letters read later by cheap post, and hand-deliver the key.
Sending the key by cheap post and checking the mailbox leaves someone stuck at the door.
Only one letter goes by cheap post; the other one could have too.
Cheap post with a courier backup for the key means paying for the courier almost every time.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think the biggest saving is the best plan. The Message Batches API is half price but has no latency promise, up to 24 hours. It fits work read later and does not fit a blocking check that people wait on.

questions.question: A new nightly job sorts each file's technical debt into classes through the Message Batches API. Each request offers a get_git_blame tool, since who changed the code and when affects the class. Every result now ends with stop_reason “tool_use”, a blame call for that file, and no class. The workflow has the repository checked out. What is the best fix?

options.t: Move the job back to real-time requests that run the tool loop, and accept the higher cost.
options.why: Works, but gives up the discount. Real-time calls run the tool loop, but every request needs the same predictable data, which can be fetched first.

options.t: Drop the blame tool, and have Claude classify each file from its content alone.
options.why: Works, but loses data. Every request finishes, but the classes ignore who changed the code and when, which the team says matters.

options.t: Answer each stopped request in a second batch, with its blame result added as a new turn.
options.why: Works, but overbuilt. A second round can finish the job, but each tool call costs another batch wait, and the data was known up front.

options.t: Run git blame before submitting, and put each file's output in its own request.
options.why: Best. A batch request cannot run a tool loop. The blame data is predictable, so supplying it up front keeps the job on the cheaper interface.

questions.decider: Every result now ends with stop_reason “tool_use”, a blame call for that file, and no class.
questions.explanation: The Message Batches API does not support multi-turn tool calling within one request. When the tool data is predictable, fetch it first and put it in the request; when it is not, use real-time requests.

eli5.question: Batch requests stop as soon as Claude asks for a tool. The clue: every request asks for the same, predictable thing, a blame for its own file, and the workflow can get it.
eli5.answer: A batch is like a letter: you can't phone mid-letter to ask a question. If you already know the writer will ask “who last changed this file?”, you put the answer in the envelope. Here that means running git blame first and putting each file's output in its request. Rule: batches can't run tool loops; if the tool data is predictable, send it in the request.
options: Switching to phone calls works, but costs double when one sheet in the envelope would do.
Removing the question means the letter is answered without facts the team says matter.
Mailing the answer back and waiting for another letter works, but it's slow and the answer was known all along.
Correct. Put the blame output in the envelope from the start.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think a batch that stops on tool_use needs a different interface. The Message Batches API cannot continue a tool loop inside one request. But when the tool data is predictable, you can fetch it first and include it, and keep the batch discount.
deep.diagram:
now:  batch req → Claude: tool_use(get_git_blame) → stops
fix:  git blame in workflow → blame text in each request
      → Claude classifies → end_turn

questions.question: The weekly report's summariser calls the Messages API. Its system prompt asks for a JSON array of risks in the reply text. Some replies will not parse: a trailing comma, an unescaped quote, or a sentence before the bracket. When that happens, the posting script drops that module from the report. Which change removes these parse failures at the source?

options.t: Define a record_risks tool whose input schema is the array, and force it in tool_choice.
options.why: Best. Tool use with a JSON schema is the most reliable way to get schema-compliant output, and it removes JSON syntax errors at the source.

options.t: Add two complete sample replies to the prompt, with escaped quotes and no text before the array.
options.why: Works, but only usually. Examples make valid JSON more likely, but nothing enforces it, and a few replies still break.

options.t: Prefill the reply with an opening bracket, and strip trailing commas before parsing.
options.why: Works, but patches symptoms. Prefill stops the preamble and the repair fixes one shape, but an unescaped quote still breaks the parse.

options.t: Retry each reply that won't parse, with the parser's error added to the request.
options.why: Works, but too late. Retry with specific errors often repairs the reply, but it pays for a second call to fix what a schema prevents.

questions.decider: Which change removes these parse failures at the source?
questions.explanation: Tool use with a JSON schema eliminates JSON syntax errors. Retries, repairs and examples treat failures after or around the fact. Values still need checking in code, since schemas don't catch semantic errors.

eli5.question: Claude writes JSON as plain text and some replies are broken: a stray comma, a quote, a sentence before it. The clue: fix it at the source, not after.
eli5.answer: Asking someone to type a table neatly still gives typos. Giving them a form with fixed boxes means the layout can't break. For the API, that form is a tool with a JSON schema: define record_risks and force it with tool_choice, and Claude's answer arrives as well-formed tool input. Rule: need valid JSON every time → tool use with a schema.
options: Correct. A form with fixed boxes; the layout can't break.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think broken JSON needs better instructions or a repair step. Those reduce or patch errors. Tool use with a JSON schema removes the whole class of syntax errors. It doesn't check the meaning of values, which still needs validation in code.

questions.question: A reviewer labelled a sample of recent review findings, and overall precision came out at 94%. The platform team now wants findings to block merges. Most findings in the sample are about null safety. Concurrency findings are rare but tied to past production incidents, and only a handful were in the sample. Only the overall figure was computed. What is the best next step?

options.t: Let findings block for a trial period, with an easy override, and track how often it is used.
options.why: Works, but too late. Override rates show some errors, but bad blocks hit real merges first, and rare categories may never show up.

options.t: Label a new sample with a quota per category, and let each block once its own precision is high.
options.why: Best. 94% is an average dominated by one common category. A quota per category measures each one, including the rare ones that matter most, before it can block.

options.t: Let only null-safety findings block for now, as they make up most of the well-scored sample.
options.why: Works, but not measured yet. It is a sensible start, but only the overall figure exists, so null safety's own precision is still unknown.

options.t: Let a finding block only when two independent review runs both report it.
options.why: Works, but measures agreement. Two runs agreeing cuts some noise, but agreement is not correctness, and it doubles the cost of a blocking check.

questions.decider: Only the overall figure was computed.
questions.explanation: Aggregate accuracy can hide weak performance in specific categories. Measure each category with stratified sampling before letting it drive an automatic decision such as blocking a merge.

eli5.question: The review scores 94% overall, and the team wants it to block merges. The clue: only the overall figure exists, and the rare, risky category barely appears in it.
eli5.answer: A school's average grade can look great while one class is failing. Before giving a class a privilege, you check that class's own grades. Here, label a new sample with a fixed number of findings from each category (stratified sampling), and let a category block merges only when its own precision is high. Rule: an average can hide a weak category; measure each one before automating it.
options: Trying it on real students and counting complaints finds problems only after they hurt someone.
Correct. Check each class's own grades before giving that class the privilege.
The big class is probably fine, but nobody has actually checked its grades.
Two teachers agreeing on a grade doesn't mean the grade is right.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think 94% overall means the review is ready to automate. An average is dominated by its biggest group. The rare concurrency category, the one tied to incidents, barely shows in it. The exam guide says to validate accuracy by type before automating, using stratified sampling.
